Run `python -u convert_data.py converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee conversion_full_out.txt`\\n4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Run `python -u train_decoder.py converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee verification_full_out.txt`. \\n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \\n7. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- `converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 9\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `converted_data.pkl` and `verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain.\\n\\n**Check 1: Output log verification**\\nRead through `verification_full_out.txt` to find and fix **all errors**. Address each warning by either fixing its cause or verifying it that it is not possible to fix it. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\\n- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\\n- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\\n- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \\n- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \\n- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \\n- Document your sanity checks to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\\n- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \\n- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \\n- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \\n- Fix any mismatches. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\\n\\n**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\\n- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference paper. \\n- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \\n- Fix any discovered issues. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\\n- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \\n- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 10\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\\n\\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Do not skip or abbreviate. Do not proceed to Step 12 until this step is completely finished.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u train_decoder.py converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \\n2. **Wait for complete execution** — this may take significant time for large datasets\\n3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \\n\\n**Done when**: \\n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `cache/` folder\\n- Create `cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. TRIAL FILTERING\n\n### 2.1 findTrials.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/findTrials.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Finds trial indices matching specified behavioral conditions\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction trialNums = findTrials(obj, conditions)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n\n1. **Extract all behavioral variables:** Uses `getStructVarNames()` to get list of trial-varying variables from `obj.bp`\n2. **Convert to columns:** Ensures all variables are column vectors (flips if rows)\n3. **Remove NaNs:** Filters NaN values from each variable\n4. **Handle frame index:** If `obj.bp.fidx` exists (indicates frame-indexed data):\n   - Sets `Ntrials` to count where `fidx==2` (valid frames)\n   - Tracks offset for `fidx==1` frames\n5. **Evaluate conditions:** For each condition string:\n   - Evaluates the condition expression (e.g., `'R&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'`)\n   - Uses `find()` to get trial indices where condition is true\n   - Handles frame index offset if present\n6. **Returns:** Cell array where each entry contains trial indices for one condition\n\n**Example conditions from getDefaultParams.m:**\n```matlab\nparams.condition(1) = {'R&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'};  % right hits, no stim, aw off\nparams.condition(2) = {'L&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'};  % left hits, no stim, aw off\n```\n\n**Available behavioral variables in obj.bp:**\n- Choice/direction: `R`, `L`\n- Outcome: `hit`, `miss`, `no` (ignore)\n- Task state: `autowater`, `stim.enable`, `early`\n- Timing: `sample`, `delay`, `goCue`\n- Licks: `ev.lickL`, `ev.lickR`\n\n---\n\n## 3. CLUSTER/NEURON FILTERING\n\n### 3.1 findClusters.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/findClusters.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Filters clusters based on quality labels\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction idx = findClusters(qualityList, qualities)\n```\n\n**Input:**\n- `qualityList`: Cell array of quality strings for all clusters (e.g., 'excellent', 'good', 'garbage')\n- `qualities`: Desired quality labels to include\n\n**Logic:**\n\n1. **Clean strings:** Removes leading/trailing spaces; converts non-string entries to ''\n2. **Special handling for 'all':** If 'all' is specified:\n   ```matlab\n   idx = find(~ismember(qualityList,'garbage') & ...\n              ~ismember(qualityList,'gabrga') & ...\n              ~ismember(qualityList,'noisy') & ...\n              ~ismember(qualityList,'real?'));\n   ```\n   Returns all clusters EXCEPT: 'garbage', 'gabrga' (typo variant), 'noisy', 'real?'\n\n3. **Handle unlabeled clusters:** Sets empty strings to 'nan'\n4. **Pattern matching:** Uses `patternMatchCellArray()` to find matching clusters\n5. **Returns:** Indices of matching clusters\n\n**Quality labels used in tutorial (getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.quality = {'all'};  % all except garbage/noisy\n```\n\n---\n\n## 4. SPIKE ALIGNMENT\n\n### 4.1 alignSpikes.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/alignSpikes.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Aligns spike times to a behavioral reference event\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction obj = alignSpikes(obj,params,prbnum)\n```\n\n**Alignment events supported:**\n\n1. **goCue:** (default) - Standard go cue event\n   - Already in `obj.bp.ev.goCue`\n\n2. **moveOnset:** Calls `findMoveOnset(obj)` (not in provided codebase)\n   - Computes time when movement begins\n\n3. **firstLick:** \n   ```matlab\n   outL = first element of lickL for each trial\n   outR = first element of lickR for each trial\n   firstLick = min(outL, outR) excluding zeros\n   ```\n\n4. **lastLick:**\n   ```matlab\n   outL = last element of lickL for each trial\n   outR = last element of lickR for each trial\n   lastLick = max(outL, outR) excluding zeros\n   ```\n\n5. **jawOnset:** Computes jaw onset from video\n   - Uses filter parameters: `f_cut=60 Hz`, `f_n=2` (filter order)\n   - Peak finding: `minpkdist=0.06s`, `minpkprom=10` (prominence threshold)\n   - Calls `alignJawOnset()` (not in provided codebase)\n\n**Alignment computation:**\n```matlab\nfor each cluster:\n    event = obj.bp.ev.(params.alignEvent)(obj.clu{prbnum}(clu).trial)\n    obj.clu{prbnum}(clu).trialtm_aligned = obj.clu{prbnum}(clu).trialtm - event\nend\n```\n\nCreates `trialtm_aligned` field for each cluster containing spike times relative to alignment event\n\n---\n\n## 5. SPIKE BINNING AND PSTH GENERATION\n\n### 5.1 getSeq.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/getSeq.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Bins spikes and computes trial-averaged PSTHs and single-trial data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction obj = getSeq(obj,params,prbnum,varargin)\n```\n\n**Input parameters:**\n- `params.tmin`, `params.tmax`: Time window bounds (e.g., -2.5 to 2.5 seconds)\n- `params.dt`: Bin width (e.g., 1/200 = 5 ms)\n- `params.smooth`: Gaussian kernel window size (bins)\n- `params.bctype`: Boundary condition type ('reflect', 'zeropad', 'none')\n- `params.cluid{prbnum}`: Cluster IDs to include\n- `params.condition`: Condition strings\n- `params.trialid`: Cell array of trial indices for each condition\n\n**Processing:**\n\n1. **Create time axis:**\n   ```matlab\n   edges = params.tmin:params.dt:params.tmax;\n   obj.time = edges + params.dt/2;\n   obj.time = obj.time(1:end-1);\n   ```\n\n2. **Initialize output matrices:**\n   ```matlab\n   obj.psth{prbnum} = zeros(numel(obj.time), numel(params.cluid{prbnum}), numel(params.condition))\n   obj.trialdat{prbnum} = zeros(numel(obj.time), numel(params.cluid{prbnum}), obj.bp.Ntrials)\n   ```\n\n3. **Compute trial-averaged PSTHs:**\n   ```matlab\n   for each cluster i and condition j:\n       trix = params.trialid{j}  % trials for this condition\n       spkix = ismember(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trial, trix)  % spikes in these trials\n       N = histc(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trialtm_aligned(spkix), edges)  % bin spike counts\n       obj.psth{prbnum}(:,i,j) = mySmooth(N./numel(trix)./params.dt, params.smooth, params.bctype)\n   ```\n   Result is in spikes/second\n\n4. **Compute single-trial data:**\n   ```matlab\n   for each cluster i and trial j:\n       spkix = ismember(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trial, j)\n       N = histc(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trialtm_aligned(spkix), edges)\n       obj.trialdat{prbnum}(:,i,j) = mySmooth(N./params.dt, params.smooth, params.bctype)\n   ```\n\n**Key computation:** Spikes binned at high resolution (1 ms), then downsampled via smoothing\n\n---\n\n## 6. LOW FIRING RATE NEURON REMOVAL\n\n### 6.1 removeLowFRClusters.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/removeLowFRClusters.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Removes neurons with low average firing rates\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [obj,cluid] = removeLowFRClusters(obj,cluid,lowFR,prbnum)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n```matlab\nmeanFRs = mean(mean(obj.psth{prbnum}, 3, 'omitnan'), 'omitnan');  % avg across time and conditions\nuse = meanFRs > lowFR;\ncluid = cluid(use);\nobj.psth{prbnum} = obj.psth{prbnum}(:,use,:);\nobj.trialdat{prbnum} = obj.trialdat{prbnum}(:,use,:);\n```\n\n**Default threshold (from getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.lowFR = 0.5;  % spikes per second\n```\n\n**Rationale:** Low-firing rate units have small observation noise in GPFA/FA models, causing artificial deflections when they spike\n\n---\n\n## 7. SMOOTHING\n\n### 7.1 mySmooth.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/utils/mySmooth.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Applies causal Gaussian smoothing to neural data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [out,kernsd] = mySmooth(x, N, varargin)\n```\n\n**Input:**\n- `x`: Data to smooth (operates on first dimension only)\n- `N`: Gaussian kernel window size (in bins)\n- `varargin`: Boundary condition type\n\n**Kernel type:** Causal Gaussian window\n\n**Logic:**\n1. If `N == 0 || N == 1`: No smoothing, return input as-is\n2. **Create Gaussian kernel:**\n   ```matlab\n   kern = gausswin(N);\n   kernsd = std(1:N);\n   kern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2)) = 0;  % Make causal (zero out first half)\n   kern = kern./sum(kern);              % Normalize\n   ```\n3. **Handle boundary conditions:**\n   - `'reflect'`: Pad N samples from beginning reflected across t=0\n   - `'zeropad'`: Pad N zeros at beginning\n   - `'none'`: No padding (default edge artifacts)\n\n4. **Apply convolution:**\n   ```matlab\n   out = conv(x_filt, kern, 'same')\n   out = out(trim:end,:)\n   ```\n\n**Default parameters (getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.smooth = 15;  % kernel window size in bins\nparams.bctype = 'none';  % boundary condition\n```\n\n**Example:** With `dt=5ms` and `smooth=15`:\n- Kernel spans 75 ms of data\n- Smoothing applied causally (kernel extends backward in time)\n\n---\n\n## 8. KINEMATICS EXTRACTION\n\n### 8.1 getKinematicsFromVideo.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/kinematics/getKinematicsFromVideo.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Extracts kinematic features (position and velocity) from video data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [kin,featLeg,nans] = getKinematicsFromVideo(obj,params)\n```\n\n**Input parameters:**\n- `params.traj_features`: Cell array of features to extract for each camera view\n- `params.alignEvent`: Event to align video to\n- `params.advance_movement`: Time offset to apply to movement data (default 0)\n\n**Default features (getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.traj_features{1} = {'tongue','left_tongue','right_tongue','jaw','trident','nose'}  % side cam\nparams.traj_features{2} = {'top_tongue','topleft_tongue','bottom_tongue','bottomleft_tongue',...\n                           'jaw','top_paw','bottom_paw','top_nostril','bottom_nostril'}  % bottom cam\n```\n\n**Processing:**\n\n1. **For each camera view and feature:**\n   ```matlab\n   [xpos{viewix}(:,:,featix), ypos{viewix}(:,:,featix)] = findPosition(...)\n   [xvel{viewix}(:,:,featix), yvel{viewix}(:,:,featix)] = findVelocity(...)\n   ```\n\n2. **Set tongue baseline position:**\n   ```matlab\n   setTongueBaselinePosition(xpos,ypos,feats,nTrials)\n   ```\n   - Computes mean initial tongue position across trials\n   - Fills NaN values in tongue position with this baseline\n   - Tracks which timepoints were NaN for later use\n\n3. **Assemble output matrix:**\n   - Creates matrix of size `(time, features*4, trials)`\n   - For each feature: `[xdisp, ydisp, xvel, yvel]`\n   - Concatenates data from both camera views\n\n**Output:**\n- `kin`: Kinematics matrix (time × features × trials)\n- `featLeg`: Legend of feature names\n- `nans`: Structure tracking NaN locations in tongue position\n\n---\n\n### 8.2 findPosition.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/kinematics/findPosition.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Extracts x,y position of a feature from video and aligns to neural time axis\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [xpos, ypos] = findPosition(taxis, obj, nTrials, view, feat, alignEv)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n\n1. **Get feature index:** `featix = findDLCFeatIndex(obj.traj, view, {feat})`\n\n2. **Get video offset:** `vidshift = findVideoOffset(obj)`\n\n3. **For each trial:**\n   - Check if video data is valid (NdroppedFrames not NaN)\n   - Create `frameTimes` if not present: `(1:nFrames)/400 Hz`\n   - Get DLC trajectory: `ts = traj(trix).ts(:, 1:2, featix)` (x,y coordinates)\n   - **Optional smoothing** (skip for tongue):\n     ```matlab\n     if ~contains(feat, 'tongue')\n         ts = mySmooth(ts, 1, 'reflect')\n     end\n     ```\n   - **Interpolate to neural time axis:**\n     ```matlab\n     tsinterp = interp1(traj(trix).frameTimes - vidshift - obj.bp.ev.(alignEv)(trix), \n                        ts, taxis)\n     ```\n   - **Fill missing values** (skip for tongue):\n     ```matlab\n     xpos(:,i) = fillmissing(xpos(:,i), 'nearest')\n     ypos(:,i) = fillmissing(ypos(:,i), 'nearest')\n     ```\n\n**Key alignment:** \n- Video timestamps are relative to bitcode start, which is offset from neural data\n- `vidshift` corrects this offset\n- Timestamps are further corrected by subtracting the alignment event time\n\n---\n\n### 8.3 findVelocity.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/kinematics/findVelocity.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Computes velocity from position using gradient\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [xvel, yvel] = findVelocity(xpos, ypos, feat)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n\n```matlab\nfor each trial:\n    tsinterp = [xpos(:,i) ypos(:,i)]\n    basederiv = median(diff(tsinterp), 'omitnan')  % baseline drift velocity\n    \n    xvel(:,i) = gradient(tsinterp(:,1))\n    yvel(:,i) = gradient(tsinterp(:,2))\n    \n    if ~contains(feat, 'tongue'):\n        xvel(:,i) = xvel(:,i) - basederiv(1)  % subtract baseline drift\n        yvel(:,i) = yvel(:,i) - basederiv(1)\n    \n    % Fill missing values (except tongue)\n    if ~contains(feat, 'tongue'):\n        xvel(:,i) = fillmissing(xvel(:,i), 'nearest')\n        yvel(:,i) = fillmissing(yvel(:,i), 'nearest')\n    else:\n        xvel(isnan(xvel(:,i)), i) = 0  % tongue velocity = 0 when invisible\n        yvel(isnan(yvel(:,i)), i) = 0\n```\n\n**Key distinctions:**\n- **Non-tongue features:** Baseline velocity subtracted (removes camera drift)\n- **Tongue:** Baseline NOT subtracted; invisible periods set to 0\n\n---\n\n## 9. MOTION ENERGY LOADING\n\n### 9.1 loadMotionEnergy.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/loadMotionEnergy.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Loads motion energy data from pre-computed .mat file and aligns to neural time axis\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction me = loadMotionEnergy(obj,meta,params,datapth,varargin)\n```\n\n**Input:**\n- `datapth`: Path to data directory\n- `varargin`: Optional `returnAfterLoad` flag (1 = return after loading, no processing)\n\n**Logic:**\n\n1. **Locate motion energy file:**\n   ```matlab\n   mepth = fullfile(datapth, 'DataObjects', meta.anm)\n   fn = patternMatchCellArray(fns, {'motionEnergy', meta.date}, 'all')\n   ```\n   Searches for file matching pattern containing both 'motionEnergy' and session date\n\n2. **Load file:**\n   ```matlab\n   me = load(fullfile(mepth, fn))\n   if isstruct(me.data)\n       me.data = me.data.data  % extract nested data if needed\n   end\n   ```\n\n3. **Interpolate to neural time axis:**\n   ```matlab\n   taxis = obj.time + params.advance_movement\n   alignTimes = obj.bp.ev.(params.alignEvent)\n   for trix = 1:numel(me.data):\n       me.newdata(:,trix) = interp1(frameTimes - vidshift - alignTimes(trix), \n                                     me.data{trix}, taxis)\n   ```\n   - Assumes `me.data` captured at 400 Hz (same as video)\n   - Aligns to neural time axis using alignment event\n   - Applies video offset correction\n\n4. **Post-processing:**\n   ```matlab\n   me.data = me.newdata\n   me.data = fillmissing(me.data, 'nearest')  % fill remaining NaNs\n   me.move = me.data > me.moveThresh  % create logical movement array\n   ```\n\n**Output:**\n- `me.data`: Motion energy time series aligned to neural time axis (time × trials)\n- `me.move`: Logical array indicating movement periods\n- `me.moveThresh`: Movement threshold value\n\n---\n\n## 10. VIDEO OFFSET COMPUTATION\n\n### 10.1 findVideoOffset.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/findVideoOffset.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Computes timing offset between neural data (Spikeglx) and video recordings\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction vidshift = findVideoOffset(obj)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n```matlab\nbitStart = mode(obj.bp.ev.bitStart);  % most common neural data start time\nvidFileOffset = mode(obj.sglx.bitcode.bitstart) / obj.sglx.fs;  % Spikeglx bitcode start time\nvidshift = vidFileOffset - bitStart;  % offset in seconds\n```\n\n**Key points:**\n- `obj.sglx.bitcode.bitstart`: Sample number where bitcode starts in Spikeglx recording\n- `obj.sglx.fs`: Spikeglx sampling rate\n- Result is in seconds\n- Uses mode to handle trial-to-trial variations\n\n---\n\n## 11. DEFAULT PARAMETERS\n\n### 11.1 getDefaultParams.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/getDefaultParams.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Defines standard parameter set for data processing\n\n**Key parameters:**\n\n```matlab\n% ALIGNMENT\nparams.alignEvent = 'goCue'  % or 'jawOnset', 'moveOnset', 'firstLick', 'lastLick'\nparams.timeWarp = 0  % piecewise linear time warping (disabled by default)\nparams.nLicks = 20   % number of licks for time warping median computation\n\n% FILTERING\nparams.lowFR = 0.5  % minimum firing rate threshold (Hz)\n\n% TRIAL CONDITIONS (binning into categories)\nparams.condition(1) = {'R&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'}  % right hits, DR\nparams.condition(2) = {'L&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'}  % left hits, DR\nparams.condition(3) = {'R&hit&~stim.enable&autowater&~early'}   % right hits, WC\nparams.condition(4) = {'L&hit&~stim.enable&autowater&~early'}   % left hits, WC\n\n% PROBE SELECTION\nparams.probe = 1  % probe number to use (1 or 2)\nparams.probeArea = 'ALM'\n\n% TIME BINNING\nparams.tmin = -2.5   % start time (seconds relative to alignEvent)\nparams.tmax = 2.5    % end time\nparams.dt = 1/200    % bin width (5 ms)\n\n% SMOOTHING\nparams.smooth = 15    % Gaussian kernel window size\nparams.bctype = 'none'  % boundary condition type\n\n% NEURON FILTERING\nparams.quality = {'all'}  % include all quality except garbage/noisy\n\n% VIDEO FEATURES\nparams.traj_features{1} = {'tongue','left_tongue','right_tongue','jaw','trident','nose'}\nparams.traj_features{2} = {'top_tongue','topleft_tongue','bottom_tongue',...}\nparams.feat_varToExplain = 80  % variance for dimensionality reduction\n\n% EPOCHS/TIMING\nparams.prep = [-2.5 -0.05]  % preparation epoch (relative to alignEvent)\nparams.move = [-2.5 1.5]    % movement epoch\nparams.advance_movement = 0.0  % time advance for movement data (seconds)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 12. SESSION DEFINITIONS\n\n### 12.1 Session Loading Functions\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/Recording and video/`\n\nSession loading functions follow pattern: `load[ANIMALID]_ALMVideo.m`\n\nEach function defines which sessions to load for an animal:\n\n**Example (loadJEB14_ALMVideo.m):**\n```matlab\nfunction meta = loadJEB14_ALMVideo(meta,datapth)\nmeta(end+1).datapth = datapth; \nmeta(end).anm = 'JEB14';\nmeta(end).date = '2022-08-22';\nmeta(end).datafn = findDataFn(meta(end));\nmeta(end).probe = 1;\nmeta(end).datapth = fullfile(meta(end).datapth,'DataObjects',meta(end).anm,meta(end).datafn);\n```\n\n**Animals with ALM+Video recordings (16 total):**\n- JEB4, JEB5, JEB6, JEB7, JEB11, JEB12, JEB13, JEB14, JEB15, JEB19, JEB23, JEB24\n- EKH1, EKH3\n- JGR2, JGR3\n\n**Metadata fields:**\n- `anm`: Animal ID\n- `date`: Session date (YYYY-MM-DD format)\n- `datafn`: Filename of data object (found via `findDataFn()`)\n- `probe`: Which probe contains ALM recording (1 or 2)\n- `datapth`: Full path to .mat file\n\n---\n\n## 13. DATA OBJECT STRUCTURE TUTORIAL\n\n### 13.1 WorkingWithDataObjs.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/WorkingWithDataObjs.m`\n\nTutorial file demonstrating how to access data. Key data structures:\n\n**obj.bp - Behavioral/task data:**\n- `obj.bp.Ntrials`: Number of trials\n- `obj.bp.hit`, `obj.bp.miss`: Outcome masks\n- `obj.bp.R`, `obj.bp.L`: Right/left choice masks\n- `obj.bp.autowater`: Whether water auto-delivered\n- `obj.bp.stim.enable`: Whether optogenetic stimulation enabled\n- `obj.bp.early`: Early lick mask\n- `obj.bp.ev`: Event timing structure\n  - `.goCue`: Go cue times (seconds)\n  - `.sample`, `.delay`: Task epoch times\n  - `.lickL`, `.lickR`: Cell array of lick times per trial\n\n**obj.clu - Spike cluster data:**\n- `obj.clu{probenum}(clusternum)` is a structure array\n- `.tm`: Spike times in session (seconds)\n- `.trialtm`: Spike times within trial (seconds)\n- `.trial`: Trial number for each spike\n- `.quality`: Quality label ('excellent', 'good', 'garbage', etc.)\n- `.spkWavs`: Spike waveforms\n- `.channel`, `.site`: Recording channel\n\n**obj.traj - DeepLabCut video tracking:**\n- `obj.traj{viewnum}(trialnum)` for camera view (1=side, 2=bottom)\n- `.ts`: Tracked coordinates (frames × [x,y,confidence] × bodyparts)\n- `.featNames`: List of tracked body parts\n- `.frameTimes`: Frame timestamps (seconds)\n- `.NdroppedFrames`: Quality indicator (NaN = bad trial)\n\n**Processed outputs (after loadSessionData):**\n- `obj.time`: Time axis aligned to alignment event (seconds)\n- `obj.psth{probenum}`: Trial-averaged PSTH (time × units × conditions)\n- `obj.trialdat{probenum}`: Single-trial binned activity (time × units × trials)\n- `obj.presampleFR{probenum}`: Baseline FR by unit and condition\n- `obj.presampleSigma{probenum}`: Baseline FR std dev\n\n---\n\n## 14. HELPER FUNCTIONS\n\n### 14.1 getStructVarNames.m\n**Purpose:** Extracts field names from obj.bp that vary trial-to-trial\n\n```matlab\nfunction varnames = getStructVarNames(obj)\n```\n\nLogic: Recursively searches obj.bp and nested structs for fields with length == Ntrials\n\n---\n\n### 14.2 patternMatchCellArray.m\n**Purpose:** Pattern matching on cell arrays of strings\n\n```matlab\nfunction [list,mask] = patternMatchCellArray(list,patterns,whichPatterns)\n```\n\nModes:\n- `'all'`: Matches cells containing ALL patterns\n- `'any'`: Matches cells in patterns list (case-insensitive)\n\n---\n\n### 14.3 findDLCFeatIndex.m\n**Purpose:** Finds index of DLC feature in obj.traj\n\n```matlab\nfunction featix = findDLCFeatIndex(traj,view,featName)\n```\n\nLogic:\n- Searches through trials to find one with valid DLC data\n- Matches feature name in that trial's `featNames` field\n- Handles partial name matches and case sensitivity\n\n---\n\n### 14.4 findDataFn.m\n**Purpose:** Locates data structure .mat file given metadata\n\n```matlab\nfunction fn = findDataFn(meta)\n```\n\nSearches directory for file matching pattern containing both:\n- `'data_structure'`\n- `meta.date`\n\nIgnores macOS hidden files (starts with `._`)\n\n---\n\n### 14.5 baselineFR.m\n**Purpose:** Computes baseline (presample) firing rates\n\n```matlab\nfunction [presampleFR, presampleSigma] = baselineFR(obj,params,prbnum)\n```\n\nLogic:\n- Time window: from `-0.5s` to mode of sample time\n- Computes PSTH for each unit and condition during this window\n- Returns median FR and std dev across time\n\n---\n\n### 14.6 findTimeIX.m\n**Purpose:** Finds time axis indices nearest to specified times\n\n```matlab\nfunction ix = findTimeIX(t, tix)\n```\n\nUses `interp1(..., 'nearest')` to find closest time values\n\n---\n\n### 14.7 getColors.m\n**Purpose:** Returns standard color scheme for plots\n\n```matlab\ncolors.rhit = [0 0 1]              % right hits = blue\ncolors.lhit = [1 0 0]              % left hits = red\ncolors.rhit_aw = [35, 166, 252]/255  % light blue\ncolors.lhit_aw = [255 142 140]/255   % light data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction obj = getSeq(obj,params,prbnum,varargin)\n```\n\n**Input parameters:**\n- `params.tmin`, `params.tmax`: Time window bounds (e.g., -2.5 to 2.5 seconds)\n- `params.dt`: Bin width (e.g., 1/200 = 5 ms)\n- `params.smooth`: Gaussian kernel window size (bins)\n- `params.bctype`: Boundary condition type ('reflect', 'zeropad', 'none')\n- `params.cluid{prbnum}`: Cluster IDs to include\n- `params.condition`: Condition strings\n- `params.trialid`: Cell array of trial indices for each condition\n\n**Processing:**\n\n1. **Create time   obj.psth{prbnum} = zeros(numel(obj.time), numel(params.cluid{prbnum}), numel(params.condition))\n   obj.trialdat{prbnum} = zeros(numel(obj.time), numel(params.cluid{prbnum}), obj.bp.Ntrials)\n   ```\n\n3. **Compute trial-averaged PSTHs:**\n   ```matlab\n   for each cluster i and condition j:\n       trix = params.trialid{j}  % trials for this condition\n       spkix = ismember(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trial, trix)  % spikes in these trials\n       N = histc(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trialtm_aligned(spkix), edges)  % bin spike counts\n       obj.psth{prbnum}(:,i,j) = mySmooth(N./numel(trix)./params.dt, params.smooth, params.bctype)\n   ```\n   Result is in spikes/second\n\n4. **Compute single-trial data:**\n   ```matlab\n   for each cluster i and trial j:\n       spkix = ismember(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trial, j)\n       N = histc(obj.clu{prbnum}(curClu).trialtm_aligned(spkix), edges)\n       obj.trialdat{prbnum}(:,i,j) = mySmooth(N./params.dt, params.smooth, params.bctype)\n   ```\n\n**Key computation:** Spikes binned at high resolution (1 ms), then downsampled via smoothing\n\n---\n\n## 6. LOW FIRING RATE NEURON REMOVAL\n\n### 6.1 removeLowFRClusters.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/removeLowFRClusters.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Removes neurons with low average firing rates\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [obj,cluid] = removeLowFRClusters(obj,cluid,lowFR,prbnum)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n```matlab\nmeanFRs = mean(mean(obj.psth{prbnum}, 3, 'omitnan'), 'omitnan');  % avg across time and conditions\nuse = meanFRs > lowFR;\ncluid = cluid(use);\nobj.psth{prbnum} = obj.psth{prbnum}(:,use,:);\nobj.trialdat{prbnum} = obj.trialdat{prbnum}(:,use,:);\n```\n\n**Default threshold (from getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.lowFR = 0.5;  % spikes per second\n```\n\n**Rationale:** Low-firing rate units have small observation noise in GPFA/FA models, causing artificial deflections when they spike\n\n---\n\n## 7. SMOOTHING\n\n### 7.1 mySmooth.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/utils/mySmooth.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Applies causal Gaussian smoothing to neural data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [out,kernsd] = mySmooth(x, N, varargin)\n```\n\n**Input:**\n- `x`: Data to smooth (operates on first dimension only)\n- `N`: Gaussian kernel window size (in bins)\n- `varargin`: Boundary condition type\n\n**Kernel type:** Causal Gaussian window\n\n**Logic:**\n1. If `N == 0 || N == 1`: No smoothing, return input as-is\n2. **Create Gaussian kernel:**\n   ```matlab\n   kern = gausswin(N);\n   kernsd = std(1:N);\n   kern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2)) = 0;  % Make causal (zero out first half)\n   kern = kern./sum(kern);              % Normalize\n   ```\n3. **Handle boundary conditions:**\n   - `'reflect'`: Pad N samples from beginning reflected across t=0\n   - `'zeropad'`: Pad N zeros at beginning\n   - `'none'`: No padding (default edge artifacts)\n\n4. **Apply convolution:**\n   ```matlab\n   out = conv(x_filt, kern, 'same')\n   out = out(trim:end,:)\n   ```\n\n**Default parameters (getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.smooth = 15;  % kernel window size in bins\nparams.bctype = 'none';  % boundary condition\n```\n\n**Example:** With `dt=5ms` and `smooth=15`:\n- Kernel spans 75 ms of data\n- Smoothing applied causally (kernel extends backward in time)\n\n---\n\n## 8. KINEMATICS EXTRACTION\n\n### 8.1 getKinematicsFromVideo.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/kinematics/getKinematicsFromVideo.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Extracts kinematic features (position and velocity) from video data\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [kin,featLeg,nans] = getKinematicsFromVideo(obj,params)\n```\n\n**Input parameters:**\n- `params.traj_features`: Cell array of features to extract for each camera view\n- `params.alignEvent`: Event to align video to\n- `params.advance_movement`: Time offset to apply to movement data (default 0)\n\n**Default features (getDefaultParams.m):**\n```matlab\nparams.traj_features{1} = {'tongue','left_tongue','right_tongue','jaw','trident','nose'}  % side cam\nparams.traj_features{2} = {'top_tongue','topleft_tongue','bottom_tongue','bottomleft_tongue',...\n                           'jaw','top_paw','bottom_paw','top_nostril','bottom_nostril'}  % bottom cam\n```\n\n**Processing:**\n\n1. **For each camera view and feature:**\n   ```matlab\n   [xpos{viewix}(:,:,featix), ypos{viewix}(:,:,featix)] = findPosition(...)\n   [xvel{viewix}(:,:,featix), yvel{viewix}(:,:,featix)] = findVelocity(...)\n   ```\n\n2. **Set tongue baseline position:**\n   ```matlab\n   setTongueBaselinePosition(xpos,ypos,feats,nTrials)\n   ```\n   - Check if video data is valid (NdroppedFrames not NaN)\n   - Create `frameTimes` if not present: `(1:nFrames)/400 Hz`\n   - Get DLC trajectory: `ts = traj(trix).ts(:, 1:2, featix)` (x,y coordinates)\n   - **Optional smoothing** (skip for tongue):\n     ```matlab\n     if ~contains(feat, 'tongue')\n         ts = mySmooth(ts, 1, 'reflect')\n     end\n     ```\n   - **Interpolate to neural time axis:**\n     ```matlab\n     tsinterp = interp1(traj(trix).frameTimes - vidshift - obj.bp.ev.(alignEv)(trix), \n                        ts, taxis)\n     ```\n   - **Fill missing values** (skip for tongue):\n     ```matlab\n     xpos(:,i) = fillmissing(xpos(:,i), 'nearest')\n     ypos(:,i) = fillmissing(ypos(:,i), 'nearest')\n     ```\n\n**Key alignment:** \n- Video timestamps are relative to bitcode start, which is offset from neural data\n- `vidshift` corrects this offset\n- Timestamps are further corrected by subtracting the alignment event time\n\n---\n\n### 8.3 findVelocity.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/kinematics/findVelocity.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Computes velocity from position using gradient\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction [xvel, yvel] = findVelocity(xpos, ypos, feat)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n\n```matlab\nfor each trial:\n    tsinterp = [xpos(:,i) ypos(:,i)]\n    basederiv = median(diff(tsinterp), 'omitnan')  % baseline drift velocity\n    \n    xvel(:,i) = gradient(tsinterp(:,1))\n    yvel(:,i) = gradient(tsinterp(:,2))\n    \n    if ~contains(feat, 'tongue'):\n        xvel(:,i) = xvel(:,i) - basederiv(1)  % subtract baseline drift\n        yvel(:,i) = yvel(:,i) - basederiv(1)\n    \n    % Fill missing values (except tongue)\n    if ~contains(feat, 'tongue'):\n        xvel(:,i) = fillmissing(xvel(:,i), 'nearest')\n        yvel(:,i) = fillmissing(yvel(:,i), 'nearest')\n    else:\n        xvel(isnan(xvel(:,i)), i) = 0  % tongue velocity = 0 when invisible\n        yvel(isnan(yvel(:,i)), i) = 0\n```\n\n**Key distinctions:**\n- **Non-tongue features:** Baseline velocity subtracted (removes camera drift)\n- **Tongue:** Baseline NOT subtracted; invisible periods set to 0\n\n---\n\n## 9. MOTION ENERGY LOADING\n\n### 9.1 loadMotionEnergy.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/loadMotionEnergy.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Loads motion energy data from pre-computed .mat file and aligns to neural time axis\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction me = loadMotionEnergy(obj,meta,params,datapth,varargin)\n```\n\n**Input:**\n- `datapth`: Path to data directory\n- `varargin`: Optional `returnAfterLoad` flag (1 = return after loading, no processing)\n\n**Logic:**\n\n1. **Locate motion energy file:**\n   ```matlab\n   mepth = fullfile(datapth, 'DataObjects', meta.anm)\n   fn = patternMatchCellArray(fns, {'motionEnergy', meta.date}, 'all')\n   ```\n   Searches for file matching pattern containing both 'motionEnergy' and session date\n\n2. **Load file:**\n   ```matlab\n   me = load(fullfile(mepth, fn))\n   if isstruct(me.data)\n       me.data = me.data.data  % extract nested data if needed\n   end\n   ```\n\n3. **Interpolate to neural time axis:**\n   ```matlab\n   taxis = obj.time + params.advance_movement\n   alignTimes = obj.bp.ev.(params.alignEvent)\n   for trix = 1:numel(me.data):\n       me.newdata(:,trix) = interp1(frameTimes - vidshift - alignTimes(trix), \n                                     me.data{trix}, taxis)\n   ```\n   - Assumes `me.data` captured at 400 Hz (same as video)\n   - Aligns to neural time axis using alignment event\n   - Applies video offset correction\n\n4. **Post-processing:**\n   ```matlab\n   me.data = me.newdata\n   me.data = fillmissing(me.data, 'nearest')  % fill remaining NaNs\n   me.move = me.data > me.moveThresh  % create logical movement array\n   ```\n\n**Output:**\n- `me.data`: Motion energy time series aligned to neural time axis (time × trials)\n- `me.move`: Logical array indicating movement periods\n- `me.moveThresh`: Movement threshold value\n\n---\n\n## 10. VIDEO OFFSET COMPUTATION\n\n### 10.1 findVideoOffset.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/funcs/findVideoOffset.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Computes timing offset between neural data (Spikeglx) and video recordings\n\n**Function signature:**\n```matlab\nfunction vidshift = findVideoOffset(obj)\n```\n\n**Logic:**\n```matlab\nbitStart = mode(obj.bp.ev.bitStart);  % most common neural data start time\nvidFileOffset = mode(obj.sglx.bitcode.bitstart) / obj.sglx.fs;  % Spikeglx bitcode start time\nvidshift = vidFileOffset - bitStart;  % offset in seconds\n```\n\n**Key points:**\n- `obj.sglx.bitcode.bitstart`: Sample number where bitcode starts in Spikeglx recording\n- `obj.sglx.fs`: Spikeglx sampling rate\n- Result is in seconds\n- Uses mode to handle trial-to-trial variations\n\n---\n\n## 11. DEFAULT PARAMETERS\n\n### 11.1 getDefaultParams.m\n**Location:** `/app/code/DataLoadingScripts/getDefaultParams.m`\n\n**Purpose:** Defines standard parameter set for data processing\n\n**Key parameters:**\n\n```matlab\n% ALIGNMENT\nparams.alignEvent = 'goCue'  % or 'jawOnset', 'moveOnset', 'firstLick', 'lastLick'\nparams.timeWarp = 0  % piecewise linear time warping (disabled by default)\nparams.nLicks = 20   % number of licks for time warping median computation\n\n% FILTERING\nparams.lowFR = 0.5  % minimum firing rate threshold (Hz)\n\n% TRIAL CONDITIONS (binning into categories)\nparams.condition(1) = {'R&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'}  % right hits, DR\nparams.condition(2) = {'L&hit&~stim.enable&~autowater&~early'}  % left hits, DR\nparams.condition(3) = {'R&hit&~stim.enable&autowater&~early'}   % right hits, WC\nparams.condition(4) = {'L&hit&~stim.enable&autowater&~early'}   % left hits, WC\n\n% PROBE SELECTION\nparams.probe = 1  % probe number to use (1 or 2)\nparams.probeArea = 'ALM'\n\n% TIME BINNING\nparams.tmin = -2.5   % start time (seconds relative to alignEvent)\nparams.tmax = 2.5    % end time\nparams.dt = 1/200    % bin width (5 ms)\n\n% SMOOTHING\nparams.smooth = 15    % Gaussian kernel window size\nparams.bctype = 'none'  % boundary condition type\n\n% NEURON FILTERING\nparams.quality = {'all'}  % include all quality except garbage/noisy\n\n% VIDEO FEATURES\nparams.traj_features{1} = {'tongue','left_tongue','right_tongue','jaw','trident','nose'}\nparams.traj_features{2} = {'top_tongue','topleft_tongue','bottom_tongue',...}\nparams.feat_varToExplain = 80  % variance for dimensionality reduction\n\n% EPOCHS/TIMING\nparams.prep = [-2.5 -0.05]  % preparation epoch (relative to alignEvent)\nparams.move = [-2.5 1.5]    % movement epoch\nparams.advance_movement = 0.0  % time advance for movement data (seconds)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 12. Key data structures:\n\n**obj.bp - Behavioral/task data:**\n- `obj.bp.Ntrials`: Number of trials\n- `obj.bp.hit`, `obj.bp.miss`: Outcome masks\n- `obj.bp.R`, `obj.bp.L`: Right/left choice masks\n- `obj.bp.autowater`: Whether water auto-delivered\n- `obj.bp.stim.enable`: Whether optogenetic stimulation enabled\n- `obj.bp.early`: Early lick mask\n- `obj.bp.ev`: Event timing structure\n  - `.goCue`: Go cue times (seconds)\n  - `.sample`, `.delay`: Task epoch times\n  - `.lickL`, `.lickR`: Cell array of lick times per trial\n\n**obj.clu - Spike cluster data:**\n- `obj.clu{probenum}(clusternum)` is a structure array\n- `.tm`: Spike times in session (seconds)\n- `.trialtm`: Spike times within trial (seconds)\n- `.trial`: Trial number for each spike\n- `.quality`: Quality label ('excellent', 'good', 'garbage', etc.)\n- `.spkWavs`: Spike waveforms\n- `.channel`, `.site`: Recording channel\n\n**obj.traj - DeepLabCut video tracking:**\n- `obj.traj{viewnum}(trialnum)` for camera view (1=side, 2=bottom)\n- `.ts`: Tracked coordinates (frames × [x,y,confidence] × bodyparts)\n- `.featNames`: List of tracked body parts\n- `.frameTimes`: Frame timestamps (seconds)\n- `.NdroppedFrames`: Quality indicator (NaN = bad trial)\n\n**Processed outputs (after loadSessionData):**\n- `obj.time`: Time axis aligned to alignment event (seconds)\n- `obj.psth{probenum}`: Trial-averaged PSTH (time × units × conditions)\n- `obj.trialdat{probenum}`: Single-trial binned activity (time × units × trials)\n- `obj.presampleFR{probenum}`: Baseline FR by unit and condition\n- `obj.presampleSigma{probenum}`: Baseline FR std dev\n\n---\n\n## 14. Quality labels match `findClusters.m` ('all' mode excludes garbage, noisy, gabrga, real?). The lowFR=1.0 Hz matches the tutorial (not getDefaultParams.m which uses 0.5 Hz). However, the FR is computed from mean of single-trial data (`trialdat`), whereas the reference code computes from the condition-averaged `psth`.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. plot(x);\n% xlim([-100 200])\n% subplot(3,1,2); plot(y)\n% xlim([-100 200])\n% subplot(3,1,3); plot(out); %hold on; plot(out,'.','MarkerSize',6)\n% xlim([-100 200])\n\n\n%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%\n\nif N == 0 || N == 1 % no smoothing\n    out = x;\n    kernsd = 0;\n    return\nend\n\nif isrow(x) % if 1-d time series, ensure column vector\n    x = x';\nend\n\nif nargin > 2\n    % handle a boundary condition\n    bctype = varargin{1};\n    if strcmpi(bctype,'reflect')\n        x_filt = cat(1,x(1:N,:),x);\n        trim = N + 1;\n    elseif strcmpi(bctype,'zeropad')\n        x_filt = cat(1,zeros(N,size(x,2)),x);\n        trim = N + 1;\n    elseif strcmpi(bctype,'none')\n        x_filt = x;\n        trim = 1;\n    else\n        warning('invalid boundary condition type - regular smoothing');\n        x_filt = x;\n        trim = 1;\n    end\nelse\n    % no bc handling\n    x_filt = x;\n    trim = 1;\nend\n\n\n\nNcol = size(x_filt, 2);\nNel = size(x_filt, 1);\n\nkern = gausswin(N);\nkernsd = std(1:N);\n\n\nkern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2)) = 0; %causal\nkern = kern./sum(kern);\n\nout = zeros(Nel, Ncol);\nfor j = 1:Ncol\n    out(:, j) = conv(x_filt(:, j), kern, 'same');\nend\nout = out(trim:end,:);\n\nend","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_23","type":"command_execution","command":"/bin/bash -lc \"sed -n '1,260p' /app/methods.txt\"","aggregated_output":"Task-switching behavioral paradigm\n\nWe designed a behavioral paradigm associated with multiple cognitive processes. In this paradigm, head-fixed mice performed two directional licking tasks that alternated block-wise within each behavioral session. These tasks varied in their cognitive demands but required the same instructed motor output.\n\nThis paradigm included an established delayed-response (DR) task in which motor planning is temporally dissociated from movement execution (Fig. 1a). In the DR task, an auditory stimulus indicated the location of a reward. After a brief delay epoch with no auditory stimuli, a separate auditory ‘go cue’ instructed the mouse to move. If the mouse performed a directional tongue movement to the correct target, a water reward was delivered. In separate blocks of trials, mice performed a water-cued (WC) task in which all auditory stimuli were omitted. Instead, a drop of water was presented at a random point in time at a randomly selected reward port. Animals consumed water upon its presentation. Mice received no explicit cues signaling DR and WC blocks. The DR task required a perceptual decision that guides the planning of a subsequent motor action. In the WC task, uncertainty in the timing and location of reward prevented formation of a motor plan before reward presentation, and, instead, mice detected reward availability using olfactory and/or vibrissal cues. This structure required animals to maintain an internal representation of the current block identity (context) to maintain high task performance.\n\nWe examined uninstructed movements in this behavioral paradigm using high-speed video. We tracked movement of the tongue, jaw, nose and paws and calculated instantaneous motion energy to quantify movement in a feature-agnostic manner (Fig. 1d–f). We found that mice performed uninstructed movements that varied in their identity and timing across both trials and contexts (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Movie 1).\n\nTo assess cortical involvement in instructed movements (directional licking) in both behavioral tasks, we used optogenetic photoinactivation to inhibit the ALM and tjM1 at the go cue (DR) or water presentation (WC) bilaterally in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (10 sessions, four mice). Simultaneous photoinactivation of both regions at the go cue (DR task) or water drop (WC task) impaired the initiation of movement in both contexts (Fig. 1b,c; all DR trials: 41 ± 20% reduction, mean ± s.d., P = 1 × 10−4; all WC trials: 15 ± 20%, P = 0.04; and Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). To assess cortical involvement in the expression of uninstructed movements, and whether these movements might be controlled by ALM or tjM1 preferentially, we bilaterally silenced the ALM or tjM1 individually during the delay epoch of DR trials (ALM: 15 sessions, tjM1: nine sessions, four mice). Uninstructed movements were suppressed by photoinactivation of either area (Extended Data Fig. 1b; ALM: 53 ± 31% reduction, mean ± s.d., P = 3 × 10−4; tjM1: 62 ± 24% reduction, P = 2 × 10−3, paired t-test) and more strongly suppressed by concurrent photoinactivation of both areas (Fig. 1g,h; 29 sessions, four mice; 73 ± 35% reduction, mean ± s.d., P = 7 × 10−9, paired t-test), similar to previous observations21 (but see ref. 34). In the DR task, delay photoinactivation of both areas led to a significant decrease in overall performance (Fig. 1i; 22% ± 14% reduction, mean ± s.d., P = 2 × 10−6 paired t-test; Extended Data Fig. 1b) as expected from the disruption of choice/planning dynamics, often leading to animals responding consistently to a preferred side rather than in a manner commensurate with the sensory cue. These results indicate that both the ALM and tjM1 are involved in the generation of uninstructed movements and the planning and execution of instructed directional tongue movements in the two-context paradigm.\n\nNeural dynamics related to task variables\n\nWhile movement-related and task-related information is encoded in both the ALM and tjM1 in the DR task and other directional licking tasks33, task variables are more strongly represented in the ALM33,36, and so we focused our subsequent analyses there. We recorded activity extracellularly in the ALM with high-density silicon probes during the two-context paradigm to track dynamics associated with planning, context and the execution of movements (Fig. 2; two-context paradigm: 12 sessions, six mice, 522 units, including 214 well-isolated single units; an additional three mice were trained only on the DR task: 25 sessions, nine mice, 1,651 units, including 483 well-isolated single units; see Extended Data Fig. 2a for per-session statistics). In the DR task, we found that choice selectivity (right versus left DR trials) was widespread across all task epochs as expected (sample: 36%; delay: 42%; response: 58% of 483 single units; 25 sessions, nine mice). Individual units showed a variety of activity patterns across trial types, including delay epoch preparatory activity, which has often been taken to be a neural signature of motor planning32,37 (Fig. 2b, left). Individual units were also selective for behavioral context during all task epochs, including during the inter-trial interval (ITI) (39% of single units, 12 sessions, six mice, 214 single units), suggesting persistent coding of context (Fig. 2b, right).\n\nMethods\n\nMouse behavior\n\nBehavioral training was conducted using custom scripts written for Bpod r0.5 (https://www.sanworks.io/shop/products.php?productFamily=bpod). All mice used in experiments were first trained on the DR task with a fixed delay epoch until they reached at least 70% accuracy. At the beginning of each trial, one of two auditory tones lasting 1.3 s was played; the tone indicating a ‘right’ trial was white noise, and the tone indicating a ‘left’ trial was a pure tone (8-kHz pulses). The delay epoch (0.9 s for 12 mice, 0.7 s for one mouse and linearly time warped to 0.9 s) started after the completion of the sample tone. After the delay epoch, an auditory go cue was played (swept-frequency cosine (chirp), 10 ms), after which animals were rewarded with approximately 3 µl of water for contacting the correct lickport. Lickport contacts before the response epoch resulted in the current task epoch restarting, ensuring that they could not progress to the next task epoch until they had stopped licking for the specified length of the current epoch. If the animal did not respond within 3 s of the go cue, this was considered an ‘ignore’ trial, although responses were typically registered within 300 ms of the go cue.\n\nMice used for the two-context task (Figs. 1, 2, 4 and 8 and Extended Data Figs. 1–3 and 9) were introduced to the WC context after they were fully trained on the DR context and at least 2 d before the first electrophysiology recording session. A behavioral session began with approximately 100 DR trials and was then followed by alternating blocks of WC and DR trials. Each interleaved block was 10–25 trials, with no fixed block duration. All sessions started with DR trials. Pilot sessions beginning with WC trials had to be terminated early due to a high ‘ignore’ rate, likely due to the mouse becoming sated early in the session. In a WC trial, all auditory cues were omitted, and an approximately 3-µl water reward was presented randomly from either lickport. Trials in which the animal contacted the lickport before the reward (‘early lick’) were omitted from analyses. ITIs were randomly drawn from an exponential distribution with mean 1.5 s. There were no explicit cues during the ITI to indicate to the animal which context block it was in.\n\nFor the randomized delay task (Fig. 3g,h,i), mice were first fully trained on the fixed delay DR task (delay duration of 0.9 s). The delay epoch length was then randomized; the duration for each trial was randomly selected from six possible values (0.3 s, 0.6 s, 1.2 s, 1.8 s, 2.4 s and 3.6 s). The probability of each delay duration being selected was assigned such that it resembled a probability density function of an exponential distribution with τ = 0.9 s, as in ref. 44. Animals were trained on this version of the task until they became experts (>70% accuracy and <20% early lick rate).\n\nVideography analysis\n\nHigh-speed video was captured (400-Hz frame rate) from two cameras (FLIR, Blackfly monochrome camera, BFS-U3-16S2M-CS). One provided a side view of the mouse, and the other provided a bottom view. We tracked the movements of specific body features using DeepLabCut (Figs. 1, 3 and 4). The tongue, jaw and nose were tracked using both cameras, whereas the paws were tracked using only the bottom view. Position and velocity of each tracked feature was calculated from each camera. The x and y position of each kinematic feature was extracted from the output of DeepLabCut. Missing values were filled in with the nearest available value for all features, except for the tongue. The velocity of each feature was then calculated as the first-order derivative of the position vector. Tongue angle and length were found using the bottom camera. Tongue angle was defined as the angle between the vector pointing from the jaw to the tip of the tongue and the vector defining the direction the mouse was facing. Tongue length was calculated as the Euclidean distance from the jaw to the tip of the tongue.\n\nMotion energy\n\nThe motion energy for a given frame and pixel was defined as the absolute value of the difference between the median value of the pixel across the next five frames (12.5 ms) and the median value of the pixel across the previous five frames (12.5 ms). Motion energy for each frame was then converted to a single value by taking the 99th percentile (~700 pixels) of motion energy values across the frame. Motion energy calculated in this manner was high during overt movements over small regions of pixel space, such as during whisking, while remaining relatively low during passive respiration that corresponded to subtle motion across the animal’s body. A threshold above which an animal was classed as moving was defined on a per-session basis manually. Motion energy distributions, per session, were bimodal, showing a large peak with little variance at low motion energy values and a second, smaller peak with high variance at large values. The threshold was set as the motion energy value separating these two modes. We found that this method of setting the threshold captured both short-duration and long-duration movements. Alternative methods, such as defining a baseline period of no movement against which to compare, were less successful due to the variability in timing of the movements across trials.\n\nPhotoinactivation experiments\n\nOptogenetic photoinactivation was deployed on approximately 30% of trials selected at random. A ‘masking flash’ (470-mm LEDs; LUXEON Rebel LED) controlled by an Arduino Teensy microcontroller (100-ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered constantly for the duration of the session to prevent mice from differentiating control and photoinactivation trials. A 488-nm laser (Coherent, OBIS 488-nm LX 150-mW laser system) was used for all photoinactivation experiments. ChR2-assisted photoinactivation (Fig. 1b,c,g and Extended Data Fig. 1b–d) was performed through a cranial window (see ‘Surgical procedures’ subsection), which replaced bone over the frontal cortex. Light was delivered either at the start of the delay epoch or at the start of the response epoch (only one epoch tested per session). A power density of 1.5 mW mm−2 was used for all photoinactivation experiments.\n\nFor delay epoch photoinactivation (Fig. 1g–i and Extended Data Fig. 1b), light was delivered at the onset of the delay epoch and lasted for 0.6 s, followed by a 0.2-s linear ramp down. We targeted one of three regions per session: bilateral motor cortex (ALM and tjM1), bilateral ALM or bilateral tjM1. A scanning galvo system (Thorlabs, GPS011) was used to simultaneously target both hemispheres by scanning at 40 Hz. The beam (2-mm diameter) was centered around the following locations: ALM (AP 2.5 mm, ML 1.5 mm), tjM1 (AP 1.75 mm, ML 2.25 mm) and motor cortex (that is, ALM and tjM1; AP 2.25 mm, ML 1.85 mm). Due to their proximity, when specifically targeting ALM or tjM1, Kwik-Cast (World Precision Instruments) was applied to the surrounding regions to prevent photoinactivation of other regions. For photoinactivation at the go cue or water drop (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1c,d), light was delivered to the motor cortex for 0.8 s, followed by a 0.2-s ramp down beginning at the go cue/water drop presentation.\n\n\nElectrophysiology recordings\n\nExtracellular recordings were performed in the ALM using one of two types of silicon probes: H2 probes, which have two shanks, each with 32 channels with 25-µm spacing (Cambridge Neurotech), or Neuropixels 1.0 (ref. 59), which have one shank and allow recording from 384 channels arranged in a checkerboard pattern (IMEC). For recordings with H2 probes, the 64-channel voltage signals were multiplexed using a Whisper recording system (Neural Circuits, LLC), recorded on a PXI-8133 board (National Instruments) and digitized at 14 bits. The signals were demultiplexed into 64 (for H2 probes) or 384 (for Neuropixels 1.0) voltage traces sampled at 25 kHz and stored for offline analysis.\n\nAt least 6 h before recording, a small craniotomy (1–1.5-mm diameter) was made over the ALM (AP 2.5 mm, ML 1.5 mm). Then, 2–5 recordings were performed on a single craniotomy on consecutive days. After inserting the probes between 900 µm and 1,100 µm (New Scale Technologies, MPM System), brain tissue was allowed to settle for at least 5 min before starting recordings. All recordings were made using SpikeGLX (https://github.com/billkarsh/SpikeGLX, phase3a release).\n\nBehavioral analysis\n\nBehavioral data were collected using Bpod r0.5 (https://www.sanworks.io/shop/products.php?productFamily=bpod). All sessions used for behavioral analysis had at least 40 correct DR trials for each direction (left or right) and 20 correct WC trials for each direction, excluding early lick and ignore trials, which were omitted from all analyses. To assess the impact of ALM photoinactivation on movement initiation, we first calculated the percent of trials with a correct lick within 600 ms of the go cue/water drop (Fig. 1c). To find the fraction of time with the tongue visible during the photoinactivation period (Extended Data Fig. 1d), for each trial we found the number of timepoints within the 1 s after the go cue/water drop where the tongue was labeled as visible by DeepLabCut and divided that by the total number of timepoints within the photoinactivation period. This was then averaged for all control or photoinactivation trials for a given session.\n\nTo assess the impact of bilateral motor cortex/ALM/tjM1 photoinactivation during the delay epoch, the average motion energy during the delay epoch was calculated separately for right and left control versus photoinactivation trials (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 1b).\n\nElectrophysiology recording analysis\n\nJRCLUST (https://github.com/JaneliaSciComp/JRCLUST, version 4.1.0) and/or Kilosort 3 (ref. 61) (https://github.com/MouseLand/Kilosort) with manual curation using Phy 2 (https://github.com/cortex-lab/phy) were used for spike sorting. A unit was considered a well-isolated single unit based on manual inspection of its inter-spike interval (ISI) histogram, separation from other units and its stationarity across the session. Units that passed manual curation but had a higher ISI violation rate were called multiunits. Recording sessions were included for analysis only if they had at least 10 units (see Extended Data Fig. 2 for a distribution of neuron counts across sessions). For the DR task, we recorded 1,651 units (483 single units) in ALM from 25 sessions using nine mice. In 12 sessions from six mice, animals performed the two-context task. In total, 522 units (214 well-isolated single units) were recorded in these sessions. Finally, for the randomized delay task, we recorded 845 units (288 well-isolated single units) in ALM from 19 sessions using four mice. For subspace alignment (Figs. 5g,n, 7d,h and 8d) and single-unit selectivity analyses (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 4c), only well-isolated single units with firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included. All units with firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included in all other analyses.\n\nTo find choice-selective neurons, 40 trials were subsampled for both right and left correct trials, and a rank-sum test was used to compare spike counts for each unit during the sample, delay or response epochs. Selective units were those with significantly different spike counts (P < 0.05) during a given epoch. Context-selective units were defined in a two-step process to ensure that we were not conflating context selectivity with slow changes in animal engagement/motivation over each session. First, 40 trials each were subsampled for DR and WC trials, and spike counts were compared (P < 0.05, rank-sum test) during the ITI (the 300 ms preceding the sample tone onset) when the animal received no external cues to indicate which context it was in. Because sessions always began with a DR block and often ended with a WC block, it is possible that differences in firing rates across contexts defined in this way could be representing time within the session. To account for this, for each unit identified in the first step, we calculated the difference in spike rate for each pair of DR and WC blocks (for example, a session with five blocks, DR–WC–DR–WC–DR, would have nPairs = 4 adjacent, overlapping block pairs) and included units as context selective only if their preferred context (context with a higher spike rate) was the same for at least nPairs − 1 of the block pairs.\n\nSelectivity in the neural population (Extended Data Fig. 4c) was calculated as the difference in spike rate on preferred − non-preferred trials in choice-selective units, with preferred trials referring to the trial type with a higher spike rate for each unit.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Selective units were those with significantly different spike counts (P < 0.05) during a given epoch. Context-selective units were defined in a two-step process to ensure that we were not conflating context selectivity with slow changes in animal engagement/motivation over each session. First, 40 trials each were subsampled for DR and WC trials, and spike counts were compared (P < 0.05, rank-sum test) during the ITI (the 300 ms preceding the sample tone onset) when the animal received no external cues to indicate which context it was in. Because sessions always began with a DR block and often ended with a WC block, it is possible that differences in firing rates across contexts defined in this way could be representing time within the session. To account for this, for each unit identified in the first step, we calculated the difference in spike rate for each pair of DR and WC blocks (for example, a session with five blocks, DR–WC–DR–WC–DR, would have nPairs = 4 adjacent, overlapping block pairs) and included units as context selective only if their preferred context (context with a higher spike rate) was the same for at least nPairs − 1 of the block pairs.\n58:Selectivity in the neural population (Extended Data Fig. 4c) was calculated as the difference in spike rate on preferred − non-preferred trials in choice-selective units, with preferred trials referring to the trial type with a higher spike rate for each unit.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}
